etymology: Hebrew Abidan (H27), my father is judge — from ab (H1), father, and din (H1777), to judge, to plead a cause, to contend for the right.
biblical_def: Abidan the son of Gideoni was prince and captain of the tribe of Benjamin during the wilderness years. The LORD named him to stand with Moses at the numbering (Num 1:11); he commanded Benjamin's camp on the west with Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Rachel keeping together (Num 2:22); he brought his tribe's offering on the ninth day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:60, 65); and he led Benjamin's host when the standards moved (Num 10:24). No word of his is recorded and no deed outside the office. The name is the substance: my father is judge. Set against Gideoni his father, whose name means hewer, the household confession runs from demolition to justice — the idols cut down, and the LORD Himself seated as the One who tries the cause. Din is not merely to pass verdict; it is to take up a case and see right done for the one who cannot get it for himself. So Abraham could ask, Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? (Gen 18:25), and Israel could sing, he cometh to judge the earth: he shall judge the world with righteousness (Psa 96:13). For a Benjamite of the wilderness generation to be called my father is judge was to say that the final word on his life would be spoken not by Egypt, nor by Canaan, nor by the congregation, but by God.
webster_summary: Prince and captain of the tribe of Benjamin in the wilderness, son of Gideoni; his name means my father is judge.

corruption_summary: Divine judgment is treated as incompatible with divine love; Scripture makes God's judging the very reason the oppressed may hope.
corruption_paragraphs: The judgment of God is the doctrine the modern mind most wishes to retire. It is presented as a relic of a harsher religion, unworthy of a God of love, and the preaching that names it is called severe. The objection misunderstands the word. Din and its Greek counterparts do not primarily mean condemnation; they mean the taking up of a case so that right is done. That is why the Psalms greet the coming Judge with singing rather than dread: let the floods clap their hands… before the LORD; for he cometh to judge the earth (Psa 98:8-9). A world in which God will not judge is a world in which every wrong done to the weak stands forever unanswered.

The doctrine is severe in exactly one direction, and Scripture does not soften it: it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment (Heb 9:27), and the judgment is according to truth. What the gospel offers is not the cancellation of the assize but a substitute at the bar — there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1), because the condemnation fell on Him. To confess with Abidan that my father is judge is therefore terror or comfort depending entirely on whether one stands in Adam or in Christ, and it is the business of preaching to make that difference plain.

etymology: Hebrew Elyasaph (H460), God has added — from El (H410), God, and yasaph (H3254), to add, to increase, to do again.
biblical_def: Two men of the wilderness generation bear this name, and Scripture keeps them apart by their fathers. The first is Eliasaph the son of Deuel, prince and captain of the tribe of Gad: named by the LORD at the numbering (Num 1:14), set over Gad's host on the south beside Reuben and Simeon (Num 2:14, where the father's name appears in its variant form Reuel), offering on the sixth day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:42, 47), and leading Gad's host at the setting forward (Num 10:20). The second is Eliasaph the son of Lael, chief of the house of the father of the Gershonites (Num 3:24), a Levite charged with the tabernacle's curtains and coverings in the march. The name both men carry is a testimony of increase: God has added. It is the same verb Rachel used when Joseph was born — The LORD shall add to me another son (Gen 30:24) — and it belongs to a generation that had watched the LORD multiply a household of seventy souls into a nation Egypt could not contain. Gad itself was named for a troop, and Jacob's blessing on Gad turned on overcoming at the last (Gen 49:19). A tribe of increase, captained by a man named for God's adding.
webster_summary: The name of two men in the wilderness: the prince of Gad, son of Deuel; and the chief of the Gershonite Levites, son of Lael. It means God has added.

corruption_summary: Increase is claimed as a promise God owes the believer; Scripture makes it a gift He sovereignly gives and sovereignly withholds.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching has made increase a transaction. God is said to be obliged to add — to income, to health, to influence — upon the believer's sowing, and the adding is measured in the coin of this world. The name Eliasaph says something both larger and humbler: that whatever is added comes from God as gift, at His discretion, for His purposes. Job confessed it in the opposite direction and was commended for it: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (Job 1:21). A doctrine of increase that cannot say the second clause is not a Christian doctrine.

Scripture's own promise of adding is real, and it is ordered. Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you (Mat 6:33) — the adding is genuine, and it is downstream of a prior seeking, and the things added are food and raiment rather than abundance. Godliness with contentment is the great gain (1Ti 6:6). The principle to recover is that the Christian is not promised more but promised enough, and is given a Father who knows what he has need of before he asks.

etymology: Hebrew Achira (H299), from ach (H251), brother, with a second element read either as ra (H7451), evil, or as rea (H7453), friend, companion — hence brother of evil or, as many read it, my brother is friend.
biblical_def: Ahira the son of Enan was prince and captain of the tribe of Naphtali in the wilderness. Named by the LORD at the numbering (Num 1:15), he commanded Naphtali on the north side with Dan and Asher (Num 2:29), offered for his tribe on the twelfth and last day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:78), and led Naphtali's host at the setting forward (Num 10:27). His place is the final one in every list: last named at the census, last to encamp, last to offer, last to march. Naphtali was the tribe of which Jacob said, Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words (Gen 49:21), and Moses blessed as satisfied with favour, and full with the blessing of the LORD (Deu 33:23). It was in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali that the great light was promised to shine on a people that walked in darkness (Isa 9:1-2), and there the Lord Jesus began to preach (Mat 4:13-16). That the last-listed tribe of the wilderness should be the first region to hear the Messiah preach is the kind of reversal Scripture delights in: the last shall be first (Mat 20:16).
webster_summary: Prince and captain of the tribe of Naphtali in the wilderness, son of Enan; last named in every list of the twelve princes.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the last place in the order is a real place, appointed and honoured by God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ahira has drawn no revisionist attention. The pressure his record exerts is on our own instincts about rank. He is twelfth of twelve at every muster, and the offering he brought on the twelfth day was, to the item, identical to the offering Nahshon of Judah brought on the first — the same charger, the same bowl, the same spoon, the same bullock and ram and lamb. Scripture spends a whole long chapter repeating the inventory twelve times rather than saying and the rest offered likewise.

That repetition is the doctrine. In the LORD's accounting the twelfth day is written out as fully as the first, because He does not weary of the obscure and does not abbreviate the faithfulness of those at the back of the line. The principle to recover is that order in the congregation is not a ranking of worth: the members should have the same care one for another, and those parts of the body which seem to be more feeble are necessary (1Co 12:22-25). A believer who serves in the twelfth position and is never called earlier has not been overlooked; he has been written down at length.

etymology: Hebrew Ammishadday (H5996), the Almighty is my kinsman, or people of the Almighty — from am (H5971), people, kindred, and Shaddai (H7706), the Almighty.
biblical_def: Ammishaddai was of the tribe of Dan in the exodus generation, and Scripture names him five times, always as the father of Ahiezer, prince and captain of Dan (Num 1:12; 2:25; 7:66, 71; 10:25). Dan's post in the order of march was the rereward — the rear guard of all the camps, the place that gathers up the stragglers and takes the first blow from behind. Ahiezer, whose name means my brother is help, commanded there; his father's name means the Almighty is my kinsman. Read together, the household confession is one of covenant kinship under God: the Almighty is not a distant power but a near relation, and therefore the rear of the column is as safe as the front. Am is the word of belonging — the word in I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God (Exo 6:7) — and to join it to Shaddai is to claim the Almighty as one's own kindred. That is not presumption; it is the covenant. Ruth's thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God (Rut 1:16) makes the same claim from the outside, and the LORD honoured it.
webster_summary: A Danite of the exodus generation, father of Ahiezer prince of Dan; his name means the Almighty is my kinsman.

corruption_summary: Nearness to God is offered as a feeling to be cultivated; the covenant makes it a legal kinship God Himself establishes.
corruption_paragraphs: Much modern devotional teaching treats intimacy with God as an atmosphere the believer produces — by music, by solitude, by the right posture of heart — and measures nearness by how near it feels. The covenant works the other way. Kinship with God is a status conferred by God and sealed by blood, and it holds when the feeling is absent. I will be to you a God, and ye shall be to me a people is a declaration, not a description of Israel's mood. Ammishaddai's name asserts a relation, and a relation either exists or it does not.

The New Testament raises the claim higher than kinsman to son. Ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father (Rom 8:15), and adoption is a legal act, irrevocable, made by the Father's will and not by the child's performance. The principle to recover is that the believer's standing does not fluctuate with his sense of it. A man marching in the rereward, at the dusty back of the column with the enemy behind him, is as truly kin to the Almighty as the man carrying the standard at the front.

etymology: Hebrew Enan (H5881), having eyes or fountain — from ayin (H5869), which in Hebrew is one word for both the eye and the spring of water.
biblical_def: Enan was a man of the tribe of Naphtali in the wilderness generation, named five times in Numbers and only ever as the father of Ahira, prince of Naphtali (Num 1:15; 2:29; 7:78, 83; 10:27). No act of his is recorded. The name rests on ayin, a word Hebrew uses for two things English keeps apart: the eye that sees and the spring that flows. The same noun stands in the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth (2Ch 16:9) and in the place-names of Israel's water — En-gedi, the spring of the kid; En-rogel; Enan itself. Both senses preach. A land that lives or dies by where the springs are learns to speak of God as a fountain: they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water (Jer 2:13). And a people camped in a wilderness under the eye of God learns that being seen is mercy, not surveillance — Hagar, alone and cast out, named the God who found her Thou God seest me (Gen 16:13). Naphtali's captain was the son of a man called eyes, or spring, and both readings are true to the God of the wilderness.
webster_summary: A man of Naphtali in the wilderness generation, father of Ahira prince of Naphtali; his name means eyes, or fountain.

corruption_summary: The all-seeing God is heard as a threat; Scripture offers His seeing first as the comfort of the afflicted.
corruption_paragraphs: An age trained to fear surveillance hears the doctrine of divine omniscience as the worst news of all — a watcher who misses nothing, keeping a record against us. Scripture knows that use of the truth and presses it on the impenitent: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do (Heb 4:13). But the first note the Bible strikes is the opposite one. The first person in Scripture to name God for His seeing is a runaway slave woman in a desert, pregnant, mistreated and utterly unrecorded by anyone else, and what she said was Thou God seest me (Gen 16:13). She meant it as rescue.

The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, and the verse says why: to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him (2Ch 16:9). Being seen by God is the ground of the afflicted believer's hope, because it means no wrong done to him in secret is unwitnessed and no faithfulness of his in obscurity is unrecorded. The principle to recover is that omniscience is a terror only to those who intend to go on sinning, and a consolation to everyone else.

etymology: Hebrew Deuel (H1845), known of God or God is knowing; the same man is called Reuel (H7467), friend of God, in Numbers 2:14, the Hebrew letters daleth and resh being closely similar in form.
biblical_def: Deuel was a man of the tribe of Gad in the exodus generation, father of Eliasaph, prince and captain of Gad (Num 1:14; 7:42, 47; 10:20). In one place, Numbers 2:14, the Authorized Version reads Eliasaph the son of Reuel, and the variation is worth facing squarely rather than hiding. The Hebrew letters daleth and resh differ only by the small turn of a stroke, and the two forms yield two good names: Deuel, known of God, and Reuel, friend of God. Both are attested elsewhere in Scripture as real Israelite names, and the man is plainly one man, identified in all four passages as the father of Eliasaph the Gadite prince. Far from embarrassing the doctrine of Scripture, the case illustrates what the doctrine actually claims: verbal plenary inspiration and inerrancy belong to the original autographs, and the providential preservation of the text through the Masoretic tradition has kept every reading open to view rather than tidied away. Nothing of doctrine or history turns on it, and both readings say something true of the same man — that the God of Israel both knows His own and calls them friends.

corruption_summary: A spelling variation is offered as proof that Scripture errs; inerrancy has always been confessed of the autographs, with the text providentially preserved in full view.
corruption_paragraphs: Cases like Deuel and Reuel are produced as evidence that the Bible contradicts itself and that any high doctrine of Scripture is therefore untenable. The argument works only against a claim no confession has ever made. What the church confesses is that the Scriptures were immediately inspired by God and by His singular care and providence kept pure in all ages — inerrancy in the original autographs, and providential preservation of the text thereafter. A variant of one letter in a proper name, transmitted openly in the tradition rather than smoothed over, is precisely what preservation without human tidying looks like.

Set the scale of the objection beside the scale of the book. The manuscripts agree on the person, the tribe, the office, the son and the sequence, and differ by one consonant in one occurrence of one name. No article of faith, no historical claim and no command is touched. Meanwhile the same textual tradition has carried the whole counsel of God — the Law, the Prophets, the Gospel — across three thousand years. A man who will not trust that record over a letter has not weighed the evidence; he has found a reason he was already looking for. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever (Isa 40:8).

etymology: Hebrew Nepheg (H5298), sprout or shoot — from a root signifying to spring up, to put forth.
biblical_def: Two men in Scripture bear this name. The first is Nepheg the son of Izhar, of the tribe of Levi, listed with his brothers Korah and Zichri in the genealogy that establishes the house of Moses and Aaron (Exo 6:21). That placing is arresting: Nepheg is brother to the Korah who led the great rebellion against Moses and Aaron and went down alive into the pit (Num 16:32-33). Scripture records no rebellion of Nepheg's. Two sons of one father, one remembered for the worst mutiny in the wilderness and one remembered only as a name in a list — and it is the quiet brother whose line is left unstained. The second Nepheg is a son of David, born to him in Jerusalem, named among Ibhar and Elishua and Japhia (2Sa 5:15; 1Ch 3:7). Of him too nothing further is told. The name means shoot or sprout, and it belongs to the family of words Scripture uses for the promised King — there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots (Isa 11:1). A son of David called sprout is a small pointer toward the Son of David who is the Branch.
webster_summary: The name of two men: a son of Izhar the Levite, brother of Korah; and a son of David born in Jerusalem. It means sprout or shoot.
webster_full: NEPHEG, Hebrew Nepheg, sprout, shoot.

Scripture records no part for him in the rebellion of Korah.
2. A son of David, born unto him in Jerusalem.
Named among the sons of David with Ibhar, Elishua and Japhia.
scriptures: Exo 6:21
And the sons of Izhar; Korah, and Nepheg, and Zichri.
Ibhar also, and Elishua, and Nepheg, and Japhia,
And Nogah, and Nepheg, and Japhia,
Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not.
corruption_summary: Family guilt is treated as inherited and inescapable; Scripture holds each soul answerable for its own sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern frameworks of inherited group guilt teach that a man carries the moral account of his house or his kind and cannot put it down. Nepheg stands against it. His brother Korah gathered two hundred and fifty princes against Moses and perished for it, and the earth closed over Korah's household; yet the children of Korah died not (Num 26:11), and Nepheg's name is written without stain in the same verse-list that names his brother. Ezekiel states the rule outright: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son (Eze 18:20).

This is not a denial that sin runs in families, nor of original sin, which Scripture teaches in Adam and which the confessions hold without flinching — all die in Adam, and every child of his comes into the world guilty and corrupt. It is a denial that the particular transgressions of a man's relations are charged to him. The two doctrines fit: guilt in Adam is universal and is answered by a second Adam; guilt for Korah's rebellion belonged to Korah. The principle to recover is that no one is trapped by his ancestry, and that the sons of Korah, whose name stands over eleven psalms, are proof that the LORD writes new records for the children of rebels.

etymology: Hebrew Pallu (H6396), distinguished or wonderful — from pala (H6381), to be marvellous, to be set apart as extraordinary; written Phallu at Genesis 46:9.
biblical_def: Pallu was the second son of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel, and head of one of the four Reubenite families — the Palluites (Gen 46:9, where the Authorized Version spells it Phallu; Exo 6:14; Num 26:5; 1Ch 5:3). He went down into Egypt with Jacob's household and his line came out at the exodus. Numbers records that his son was Eliab, and Eliab's sons were Nemuel, Dathan and Abiram — that Dathan and Abiram, which were famous in the congregation, who strove against Moses and against Aaron in the company of Korah (Num 26:9). So the house named wonderful produced, within two generations, two of the ringleaders of the rebellion that the earth swallowed. The irony is not accidental to the way Scripture tells Reuben's story. Reuben was the firstborn with every natural advantage — the excellency of dignity, and the excellency of power — and lost it by instability (Gen 49:3-4). A tribe of distinguished beginnings and forfeited inheritance is the standing warning of the Pentateuch that birthright is not character, and that a good name handed down is a trust rather than a possession.
webster_summary: Second son of Reuben and head of the family of the Palluites; his name means distinguished or wonderful.

corruption_summary: A distinguished name is mistaken for a settled standing; Scripture makes every generation answer for itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Covenant privilege is easily misread as covenant safety. Israel made that mistake constantly — We have Abraham to our father (Mat 3:9) — and John the Baptist answered that God is able of stones to raise up children unto Abraham. The house of Pallu had privilege in abundance: descent from the firstborn of Israel, a name meaning distinguished, a place in the households that came out of Egypt under the blood of the lamb. Two generations later its most famous members are Dathan and Abiram, standing at their tent doors in open defiance of the man God had sent.

The corollary is the sober doctrine of the visible church. Baptism does not regenerate; a Christian household does not guarantee a Christian child; membership is not the same as union with Christ. They are not all Israel, which are of Israel (Rom 9:6). What the privilege does is set a child under the means of grace — preaching, ordinance, family instruction — which God ordinarily uses and which no child may presume upon. The principle to recover is that every generation must be converted for itself, and that a name like Pallu is an obligation rather than an inheritance.

etymology: Hebrew Chanok (H2585), dedicated or initiated — from chanak (H2596), to dedicate, to initiate, to train up; the same root that gives the feast of dedication its name.
biblical_def: Hanoch is the Authorized Version's form of a name it elsewhere renders Enoch, and it belongs in Scripture to two men distinct from Enoch the son of Jared who walked with God. The first is Hanoch the eldest son of Reuben, head of the family of the Hanochites, who went down into Egypt with Jacob and whose house was numbered in the wilderness (Gen 46:9; Num 26:5; 1Ch 5:3). The second is Hanoch a son of Midian, grandson of Abraham by Keturah, listed among the Arabian peoples descended from the patriarch (Gen 25:4; written Henoch at 1Ch 1:33). The name means dedicated, from chanak — the verb behind the dedication of a house (Deu 20:5), behind Hanukkah, the feast of the dedication of the temple, and behind the great charge to fathers: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it (Pro 22:6). The word in that proverb is this word. To name a son Hanoch was to declare him set apart for God from the beginning, and to take on the work of training that the setting apart implies.
webster_summary: The name of two men — the eldest son of Reuben, and a son of Midian by Keturah. It means dedicated, or trained up.

corruption_summary: Proverbs 22:6 is read as a guarantee of outcomes; the verb means to dedicate and train, and the proverb states a rule, not a contract.
corruption_paragraphs: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it has been pressed into service as an absolute promise, with the result that faithful parents of wayward children are handed a verdict of guilt they do not deserve, and presumptuous parents are handed an assurance they have no right to. A proverb is a proverb. The book of Proverbs states the ordinary course of things under God's moral government — diligence tends to profit, a soft answer tends to turn away wrath — and it is not a set of mechanical guarantees, as the book of Job and the psalms of the afflicted righteous exist in part to show.

Held rightly, the verse is a mercy. Chanak means to dedicate and to initiate: to set a child apart for God and to start him along a path, which is exactly what Christian parents are commanded to do — bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Eph 6:4). The outcome remains God's to give, for regeneration is His work and not the parent's; the training is the parent's to do, and it is not optional. The principle to recover is the division of labour: parents are responsible for the means, God is sovereign over the end, and a father who has been faithful in the first is not guilty for the second.

etymology: Hebrew Libni (H3845), white — from laban (H3835), to be white, to make white; the root behind Lebanon, the white mountain, and behind lebonah, frankincense.
biblical_def: Libni was the elder son of Gershon, the firstborn of Levi, and head of the Levitical family of the Libnites (Exo 6:17; Num 3:18, 21; 1Ch 6:17, 20). The Gershonites were not priests; their charge in the wilderness was the fabric of the sanctuary — the curtains of the tabernacle, the covering, the hanging for the door, the hangings of the court and their cords. They carried the cloth. It was heavy, unglamorous work, done under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron, and it was appointed by name. The name Libni means white, from the root that gives Lebanon its name and frankincense its name, and it sits well on a house whose whole business was the white linen of the LORD's dwelling. Fine twined linen was the material of the court hangings and of the priestly garments, and the New Testament takes up the figure without alteration: the Lamb's wife is arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints (Rev 19:8). A Levite named white, keeping the white curtains of the sanctuary, is a small picture of the whole ministry of the church — entrusted with what is holy, and answerable for keeping it clean.

corruption_summary: Unseen service is ranked below visible ministry; Scripture appoints the carriers of the curtains by name and by charge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No movement disputes Libni. What disputes him is the instinct in every congregation that ranks ministries by visibility — the pulpit above the nursery, the platform above the chairs that get stacked, the named above the unnamed. Israel had a built-in rebuke to it. The Kohathites bore the ark and the holy vessels; the Gershonites bore the cloth; the Merarites bore the boards and sockets and pins. All three were numbered by name, charged by Moses, assigned by the word of the LORD, and none of them chose his own portion.

The apostle presses the same point on the church: the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee, and those members which seem to be more feeble are necessary (1Co 12:21-22). The principle to recover is that in the LORD's house the assignment, not the prominence, is what makes a work holy. A man who carries the curtains because God appointed him to carry the curtains is doing sanctuary service as truly as the man who carries the ark, and he will be judged by the same standard: it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful (1Co 4:2).
